claim: hKif15 is a plus-end-directed processive homotetramer.
source: We reveal that hKif15 is a plus-end-directed processive homotetramer that can step against loads of up to 3.5 pN.
evidence: Supported by biochemical analysis (native PAGE, glycerol gradients, SEC-MALS), photobleaching experiments showing up to 4 eGFP molecules, and single-molecule TIRF microscopy showing processive plus-end-directed movement.

claim: hKif15 can step against loads of up to 3.5 pN.
source: We reveal that hKif15 is a plus-end-directed processive homotetramer that can step against loads of up to 3.5 pN.
evidence: Demonstrated by optical trap experiments showing motor detachment at loads between 1.5 and 3.5 pN.

claim: hKif15 is the first kinesin that effectively switches microtubule tracks at intersections.
source: We further show that hKif15 is the first kinesin that effectively switches microtubule tracks at intersections, enabling it to navigate microtubule networks, such as the spindle.
evidence: Supported by TIRF microscopy showing that every fifth motor switches tracks at intersections, with quantification showing equal likelihood of pass, switch, pause, and dissociation events.

claim: hKif15 tetramers are capable of cross-linking microtubules.
source: hKif15 tetramers are also capable of cross-linking microtubules, but unexpectedly, this does not depend on hTpx2.
evidence: Demonstrated by experiments showing hKif15 can mediate microtubule-microtubule cross-linking in the absence of hTpx2.

claim: hKif15 microtubule cross-linking does not depend on hTpx2.
source: hKif15 tetramers are also capable of cross-linking microtubules, but unexpectedly, this does not depend on hTpx2.
evidence: Shown by experiments demonstrating hKif15 can cross-link microtubules on its own without hTpx2.

claim: hTpx2 inhibits hKif15 stepping when microtubule-bound.
source: Instead, we find that hTpx2 inhibits hKif15 stepping when microtubule-bound.
evidence: Demonstrated by TIRF microscopy showing 70% reduction in motile motors and optical trap experiments showing loss of processive stepping in presence of hTpx2.

claim: hKif15 is a second tetrameric spindle motor in addition to the kinesin-5 Eg5.
source: Our data reveal that hKif15 is a second tetrameric spindle motor in addition to the kinesin-5 Eg5 and provides insight into the mechanisms by which hKif15 and its inhibitor hTpx2 modulate spindle microtubule architecture.
evidence: Supported by biochemical characterization showing tetrameric organization and functional studies in spindle context.

claim: Kif11 (Eg5) is a homotetrameric plus-end-directed molecular motor.
source: Initial assembly of the spindle requires the separation of centrosomes by the homotetrameric plus-end-directed molecular motor Kif11 (Eg5)—a member of the kinesin-5 family (Tanenbaum and Medema, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Kif11 can drive the outward sliding of anti-parallel microtubules.
source: In vitro reconstitution experiments reveal that Kif11 can drive the outward sliding of anti-parallel microtubules thus providing a mechanistic basis for centrosome separation (Kapitein et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to published in vitro reconstitution experiments.

claim: Kif11 is not required to maintain spindle bipolarity due to the compensatory activity of Kif15.
source: Although essential for centrosome separation, Kif11 is not required to maintain subsequent spindle bipolarity due to the compensatory activity of the Kinesin-12 Kif15 (hKlp2) (Tanenbaum et al., 2009; Vanneste et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to published cell biological studies.

claim: Overexpression of hKif15 can overcome the absolute requirement for hKif11 in centrosome separation.
source: Furthermore, overexpression of hKif15 can overcome the absolute requirement for hKif11 in centrosome separation (Tanenbaum et al., 2009; Sturgill and Ohi, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Xenopus Kinesin-12 (xKlp2) is a dimeric plus-end-directed motor.
source: Kinesin-12 proteins from Xenopus (xKlp2)(Wittmann et al., 1998), sea urchin (Rogers et al., 2000), and rat (Liu et al., 2010) are dimeric plus-end-directed motors that are targeted to the spindle by the microtubule-associated protein (MAP) Tpx2 (targeting protein for xKlp2) (Wittmann et al., 1998).
evidence: Supported by citation to published characterization.

claim: Sea urchin Kinesin-12 is a dimeric plus-end-directed motor.
source: Kinesin-12 proteins from Xenopus (xKlp2)(Wittmann et al., 1998), sea urchin (Rogers et al., 2000), and rat (Liu et al., 2010) are dimeric plus-end-directed motors that are targeted to the spindle by the microtubule-associated protein (MAP) Tpx2 (targeting protein for xKlp2) (Wittmann et al., 1998).
evidence: Supported by citation to published characterization.

claim: Rat Kinesin-12 is a dimeric plus-end-directed motor.
source: Kinesin-12 proteins from Xenopus (xKlp2)(Wittmann et al., 1998), sea urchin (Rogers et al., 2000), and rat (Liu et al., 2010) are dimeric plus-end-directed motors that are targeted to the spindle by the microtubule-associated protein (MAP) Tpx2 (targeting protein for xKlp2) (Wittmann et al., 1998).
evidence: Supported by citation to published characterization.

claim: Kinesin-12 proteins are targeted to the spindle by the microtubule-associated protein Tpx2.
source: Kinesin-12 proteins from Xenopus (xKlp2)(Wittmann et al., 1998), sea urchin (Rogers et al., 2000), and rat (Liu et al., 2010) are dimeric plus-end-directed motors that are targeted to the spindle by the microtubule-associated protein (MAP) Tpx2 (targeting protein for xKlp2) (Wittmann et al., 1998).
evidence: Supported by citation to published studies.

claim: hKif15 is recruited to the spindle microtubules by hTpx2 in human cells.
source: hKif15 is also recruited to the spindle microtubules by hTpx2 in human cells (Tanenbaum et al., 2009; Vanneste et al., 2009) with the interaction between dimeric hKif15 and hTpx2 hypothesised to enable the motor to cross-link and slide anti-parallel microtubules (Tanenbaum et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to published cell biological studies.

claim: hKif15 localizes to kinetochore (k)-fibres.
source: However, this model has been challenged by recent cell-biological studies showing that hKif15 localizes to kinetochore (k)-fibres (parallel microtubule bundles) and contributes to the generation of forces that counter those generated by hKif11 (Sturgill and Ohi, 2013; Vladimirou et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to published cell biological studies.

claim: hKif15 contributes to the generation of forces that counter those generated by hKif11.
source: However, this model has been challenged by recent cell-biological studies showing that hKif15 localizes to kinetochore (k)-fibres (parallel microtubule bundles) and contributes to the generation of forces that counter those generated by hKif11 (Sturgill and Ohi, 2013; Vladimirou et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies.

claim: hKif15 is emerging as a potentially important therapeutic target.
source: hKif15 is therefore emerging as a potentially important therapeutic target (Groen, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature.

claim: His6-hKif15 migrates at approximately 730 kDa on native PAGE.
source: Analysis of His6-hKif15 on native PAGE revealed that the protein migrates at ∼730 KDa (Figure 1B).
evidence: Demonstrated by native PAGE analysis shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The predicted molecular weight of His6-hKif15 is 164.8 kDa.
source: Given the predicted molecular weight of His6-hKif15 (164.8 kDa) our data suggest the presence of hKif15 tetramers, although hydrodynamic analysis of the frog (xKlp2) and Sea urchin (KRP180) Kif15 orthologues indicated that the motor is dimeric with a sedimentation coefficient of 8.1S and 8.3S respectively (Wittmann et al., 1998; Rogers et al., 2000).
evidence: Based on sequence analysis and calculation.

claim: Frog xKlp2 has a sedimentation coefficient of 8.1S.
source: Given the predicted molecular weight of His6-hKif15 (164.8 kDa) our data suggest the presence of hKif15 tetramers, although hydrodynamic analysis of the frog (xKlp2) and Sea urchin (KRP180) Kif15 orthologues indicated that the motor is dimeric with a sedimentation coefficient of 8.1S and 8.3S respectively (Wittmann et al., 1998; Rogers et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by citation to published hydrodynamic analysis.

claim: Sea urchin KRP180 has a sedimentation coefficient of 8.3S.
source: Given the predicted molecular weight of His6-hKif15 (164.8 kDa) our data suggest the presence of hKif15 tetramers, although hydrodynamic analysis of the frog (xKlp2) and Sea urchin (KRP180) Kif15 orthologues indicated that the motor is dimeric with a sedimentation coefficient of 8.1S and 8.3S respectively (Wittmann et al., 1998; Rogers et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by citation to published hydrodynamic analysis.

claim: At physiological ionic strengths, His6-hKif15 and His6-hKif15-eGFP have apparent sedimentation coefficients of approximately 12S.
source: At physiological ionic strengths (35 mM sodium phosphate buffer, 0-150 mM NaCl) both His6-hKif15 and His6-hKif15-eGFP appear to be monodispersed and have apparent sedimentation coefficients of ∼12S (Figure 1C).
evidence: Demonstrated by glycerol gradient ultracentrifugation shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Increasing salt concentration to 300 mM NaCl converts hKif15 into a species that runs at approximately 8S.
source: However, increasing the salt concentration to 300 mM NaCl converts hKif15 into a species that runs at ∼8S (Figure 1C).
evidence: Demonstrated by glycerol gradient ultracentrifugation at different salt concentrations shown in Figure 1C.

claim: hKif15 exists as a tetramer at physiological ionic strength that can be forced to dissociate into a dimer at high ionic strength.
source: Taken together, our data show that hKif15 exists as a tetramer at physiological ionic strength that can be forced to dissociate into a dimer at high ionic strength.
evidence: Based on glycerol gradient data showing 12S at physiological salt and 8S at high salt.

claim: SEC-MALS analysis confirmed the presence of tetrameric hKif15 motors with a molecular weight of 744.4 ± 14.1 kDa.
source: This analysis confirmed the presence of tetrameric hKif15 motors (molecular weight of 744.4 ± 14.1 kDa) (Figure 1D, 1st peak, blue line).
evidence: Demonstrated by SEC-MALS analysis shown in Figure 1D.

claim: SEC-MALS detected a dimeric population of hKif15 motors with a molecular weight of 360.1 ± 6.5 kDa.
source: We could also detect a dimeric population of motors (molecular weight of 360.1 ± 6.5 kDa) indicating that there is some degree of complex dissociation in solution under these conditions (Figure 1D, 2nd peak, orange line).
evidence: Demonstrated by SEC-MALS analysis shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The majority of hKif15 motors move either by directional movement towards the plus-end or by bidirectional 1D-diffusion along the microtubule lattice.
source: The majority hKif15 motors move either by directional movement towards the plus-end of individual microtubules (Figure 2A, 'P') or by bidirectional 1D-diffusion (Figure 2A, 'D', Figure 2B, right, Figure 2—figure supplement 1D, right) along the microtubule lattice.
evidence: Demonstrated by TIRF microscopy observations shown in Figure 2A and related figures.

claim: Processive and diffusive movement types are equally likely at all salt conditions tested.
source: These types of movement are equally likely at all salt conditions tested (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A) and single motors can switch between both modes (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Demonstrated by TIRF microscopy at different salt concentrations shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Single hKif15 motors can switch between processive and diffusive modes.
source: These types of movement are equally likely at all salt conditions tested (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A) and single motors can switch between both modes (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Demonstrated by TIRF microscopy showing mode switching in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Processively moving, plus-end-directed hKif15 motors move at a speed of 137.8 ± 4.1 nm•s−1 (median ± SEM).
source: Processively moving, plus-end-directed motors move at a speed of 137.8 ± 4.1 nm•s−1 median ± SEM, though we observed velocities up to 550 nm•s−1 (Figure 2B, left).
evidence: Measured by TIRF microscopy with velocity distribution shown in Figure 2B, left.

claim: hKif15 velocities up to 550 nm•s−1 have been observed.
source: Processively moving, plus-end-directed motors move at a speed of 137.8 ± 4.1 nm•s−1 median ± SEM, though we observed velocities up to 550 nm•s−1 (Figure 2B, left).
evidence: Measured by TIRF microscopy with velocity distribution shown in Figure 2B, left.

claim: The run length of hKif15 motors is 1.9 ± 0.09 µm (median ± SEM) with a maximum of 9.6 µm.
source: The run length of hKif15 motors is 1.9 ± 0.09 µm median ± SEM (max. 9.6 µm) (Figure 2B, middle) and their residency time 26.3 ± 2.8 s median ± SEM (max. >180 s) (Figure 2B, right).
evidence: Measured by TIRF microscopy with run length distribution shown in Figure 2B, middle.

claim: The residency time of hKif15 motors is 26.3 ± 2.8 s (median ± SEM) with a maximum greater than 180 s.
source: The run length of hKif15 motors is 1.9 ± 0.09 µm median ± SEM (max. 9.6 µm) (Figure 2B, middle) and their residency time 26.3 ± 2.8 s median ± SEM (max. >180 s) (Figure 2B, right).
evidence: Measured by TIRF microscopy with residency time distribution shown in Figure 2B, right.

claim: Processive runs of hKif15 can include pauses up to 20.5 s with a median of 5.0 ± 0.4 s.
source: Processive runs can include pauses up to 20.5 s (median ± SEM: 5.0 ± 0.4 s) at a frequency of 0.30 ± 0.04 pauses•µm−1 mean ± SD (n = 162, three different experiments) without motor-dissociation from the microtubule lattice (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B,D, middle).
evidence: Measured by TIRF microscopy with pause analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B,D.

claim: hKif15 pauses occur at a frequency of 0.30 ± 0.04 pauses•µm−1 (mean ± SD).
source: Processive runs can include pauses up to 20.5 s (median ± SEM: 5.0 ± 0.4 s) at a frequency of 0.30 ± 0.04 pauses•µm−1 mean ± SD (n = 162, three different experiments) without motor-dissociation from the microtubule lattice (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B,D, middle).
evidence: Measured by TIRF microscopy across three experiments with n=162.

claim: More than 90% of hKif15 motors remain attached when they reach the microtubule end.
source: Additionally, when motors reach the microtubule end, more than 90% remain attached (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D, left note orange column).
evidence: Quantified by TIRF microscopy shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D, left.

claim: hKif15 motors dwell at the microtubule tip for 18.8 ± 3.5 s (median ± SEM) with a maximum greater than 152 s.
source: Motors dwell at the tip for 18.8 ± 3.5 s median ± SEM (max. >152 s) (Figure 2A, (asterix), Figure 2—figure supplement 1D, left) and may switch to diffusional movement on the end-proximal microtubule lattice (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Measured by TIRF microscopy with dwell time analysis shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: hKif15 motors may switch to diffusional movement on the end-proximal microtubule lattice after reaching the tip.
source: Motors dwell at the tip for 18.8 ± 3.5 s median ± SEM (max. >152 s) (Figure 2A, (asterix), Figure 2—figure supplement 1D, left) and may switch to diffusional movement on the end-proximal microtubule lattice (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Observed by TIRF microscopy shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: 87.5% of hKif15 motors are plus-end-directed and 12.5% are minus-end-directed (n = 504).
source: While the majority of hKif15 motors either moves directionally to the plus-end or diffuses along the lattice, we also observed a small proportion of motors that move processively towards the minus-end of polarity-marked microtubules (87.5% plus-end-directed motors vs 12.5% minus-end-directed motors, n = 504) (Figure 2A, right kymograph, 'MP').
evidence: Quantified by TIRF microscopy of polarity-marked microtubules shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Minus-end-directed hKif15 motors move at a speed similar to plus-end-directed motors.
source: Minus-end-directed motors move at a speed similar to plus-end-directed motors, but have a significantly reduced run length/residency time and do not undergo directional reversals (Figure 2C).
evidence: Measured by TIRF microscopy with velocity distribution shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Minus-end-directed hKif15 motors have a significantly reduced run length/residency time compared to plus-end-directed motors.
source: Minus-end-directed motors move at a speed similar to plus-end-directed motors, but have a significantly reduced run length/residency time and do not undergo directional reversals (Figure 2C).
evidence: Measured by TIRF microscopy with run length and residency time distributions shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Minus-end-directed hKif15 motors do not undergo directional reversals.
source: Minus-end-directed motors move at a speed similar to plus-end-directed motors, but have a significantly reduced run length/residency time and do not undergo directional reversals (Figure 2C).
evidence: Observed by TIRF microscopy analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Both processive and diffusive hKif15 motors bleach in up to four steps.
source: This analysis showed that both processive and diffusive motors bleach in up to four steps, indicating the presence of four eGFP molecules per motor (Figure 2D).
evidence: Demonstrated by photobleaching analysis shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Processive hKif15 tetramers are evident throughout the velocity distribution.
source: Furthermore, processive tetramers are evident throughout the velocity distribution (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Demonstrated by photobleaching analysis of motors at different velocities shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1E.

claim: hKif15 motors make processive steps along the microtubule before detaching at relatively low loads between 1.5 and 3.5 pN.
source: Figure 2E shows two position traces in which hKif15 motors make a number of processive steps along the microtubule before detaching at relatively low loads between 1.5 and 3.5 pN.
evidence: Demonstrated by optical trap experiments shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Beads linked to hKif15 can move out of the trap before moving back in the opposite direction without detaching.
source: We also observed that beads move out the trap before moving back in the opposite direction without detaching (green arrowhead).
evidence: Observed in optical trap experiments shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Bidirectional bead movements in the trap may reflect the minus- and plus-end-directed diffusive motion observed in TIRF experiments.
source: These events may reflect the minus- and plus-end-directed diffusive motion observed in our TIRF experiments (Figure 2A).
evidence: Inferred from comparison of optical trap and TIRF observations.

claim: hKif15 undergoes diffusive movement along microtubules, processive plus-end-directed stepping over long-distances, or short duration movements to the minus-end.
source: Together with our TIRF microscopy, we conclude that hKif15 is a homotetramer that undergoes either diffusive movement along microtubules, processive plus-end-directed stepping over long-distances or short duration movements to the minus-end.
evidence: Conclusion based on combined TIRF microscopy and optical trap data.

claim: Kinesin-1 normally passes intersections and only in rare cases pauses or switches microtubule tracks.
source: The well-studied kinesin-1 will normally pass intersections and only in rare cases the motor will pause or switch microtubule tracks (Ross et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to published study.

claim: hKif15 motors show significantly elevated pause and switch events at intersections compared to kinesin-1.
source: In contrast, hKif15 motors show significantly elevated pause and switch events at intersections.
evidence: Inferred from comparison with kinesin-1 behavior and quantification of hKif15 behavior at intersections.

claim: Every fifth hKif15 motor that approaches an intersection switches its microtubule track.
source: Every fifth motor that approaches an intersection switches its microtubule track (Figure 3A,B; Videos 1 and 2).
evidence: Quantified by TIRF microscopy shown in Figure 3B.

claim: All events at intersections (pass, switch, pause, and dissociation) are equally likely for hKif15.
source: In general all events—pass, switch, pause, and dissociation at intersections—are equally likely.
evidence: Quantified by TIRF microscopy shown in Figure 3B.

claim: hKif15 is able to roam microtubule networks.
source: In this way, hKif15 is able to roam microtubule networks and Figure 3C demonstrates that one tetramer (see bleaching steps, lower panel) can indeed navigate along several different microtubules: the motor starts processive movement on microtubule #1 (trace A), eventually dissociates and rebinds to microtubule #2.
evidence: Demonstrated by TIRF microscopy tracking a single motor across multiple microtubules shown in Figure 3C.

claim: A single hKif15 tetramer can navigate along several different microtubules.
source: In this way, hKif15 is able to roam microtubule networks and Figure 3C demonstrates that one tetramer (see bleaching steps, lower panel) can indeed navigate along several different microtubules: the motor starts processive movement on microtubule #1 (trace A), eventually dissociates and rebinds to microtubule #2. On this, the motor diffuses a short distance (trace B) and dissociates again, just to rebind to microtubule #1. It processively follows microtubule #1 (trace C) and sequentially switches to microtubules #3 (trace D) and #4 (trace E), ending at the plus-end of microtubule #4 without detaching from the microtubule lattice(s) once again (see also Video 3).
evidence: Demonstrated by TIRF microscopy tracking shown in Figure 3C and Video 3.

claim: Kif15 is a processive motor that is able to navigate microtubule networks by effectively switching microtubule tracks.
source: Thus, Kif15 is a processive motor that is able to navigate microtubule networks by effectively switching microtubule tracks.
evidence: Conclusion based on TIRF microscopy data showing track switching and network navigation.

claim: hKif15 can mediate the cross-linking of microtubules on its own.
source: By drawing kymographs, we found that hKif15 could mediate the cross-linking of microtubules (Figure 4) on its own, but that there was very little microtubule–microtubule sliding activity.
evidence: Demonstrated by TIRF microscopy experiments with surface-bound and cargo microtubules shown in Figure 4.

claim: There is very little microtubule-microtubule sliding activity by hKif15.
source: By drawing kymographs, we found that hKif15 could mediate the cross-linking of microtubules (Figure 4) on its own, but that there was very little microtubule–microtubule sliding activity.
evidence: Observed by TIRF microscopy shown in Figure 4.

claim: hKif15 shows episodes of bidirectional short duration sliding indicating a tug-of-war.
source: Besides pivoting microtubules, we did observe episodes of bidirectional short duration sliding indicating a tug-of-war (Figure 4, right) and rarely the transport of short microtubules (Figure 4, left): behaviours that were recently reported for the yeast Kinesin-8 Kip3 (Su et al., 2013).
evidence: Observed by TIRF microscopy shown in Figure 4, right.

claim: hKif15 rarely transports short microtubules.
source: Besides pivoting microtubules, we did observe episodes of bidirectional short duration sliding indicating a tug-of-war (Figure 4, right) and rarely the transport of short microtubules (Figure 4, left): behaviours that were recently reported for the yeast Kinesin-8 Kip3 (Su et al., 2013).
evidence: Observed by TIRF microscopy shown in Figure 4, left.

claim: Yeast Kinesin-8 Kip3 shows tug-of-war and microtubule transport behaviors.
source: Besides pivoting microtubules, we did observe episodes of bidirectional short duration sliding indicating a tug-of-war (Figure 4, right) and rarely the transport of short microtubules (Figure 4, left): behaviours that were recently reported for the yeast Kinesin-8 Kip3 (Su et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to published study.

claim: There is no clear evidence that hKif15 can drive continuous extensile sliding of anti-parallel microtubule bundles like hKif11.
source: However, we have no clear evidence to support the idea that hKif15 can drive continuous extensile sliding of anti-parallel microtubule bundles like hKif11.
evidence: Based on lack of observation of continuous sliding in microtubule cross-linking and gliding assays.

claim: hKif15 motors frequently pause during processive excursions on the lattice and dwell at the ends for a long period.
source: This is presumably because the motors frequently pause during processive excursions on the lattice and dwell at the ends for a long period (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B–D).
evidence: Observed by TIRF microscopy shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B–D.

claim: hKif15 shows discontinuous short distance movement and pivoting of microtubules on surface-bound motors.
source: Consistent with this, we only observed discontinuous short distance movement and pivoting of microtubules (around their ends) on surface-bound hKif15 motors, but not continuous microtubule sliding in microtubule gliding assays (Videos 4 and 5).
evidence: Observed in microtubule gliding assays shown in Videos 4 and 5.

claim: hKif15 does not show continuous microtubule sliding in microtubule gliding assays.
source: Consistent with this, we only observed discontinuous short distance movement and pivoting of microtubules (around their ends) on surface-bound hKif15 motors, but not continuous microtubule sliding in microtubule gliding assays (Videos 4 and 5).
evidence: Observed in microtubule gliding assays shown in Videos 4 and 5.

claim: hTpx2 is not required for hKif15 to bind microtubules.
source: So far our experiments show that hTpx2 is not required for hKif15 to bind microtubules or for the motors processivity and ability to crosslink microtubules (as a tetramer).
evidence: Based on experiments showing hKif15 can bind, move processively, and crosslink microtubules in the absence of hTpx2.

claim: hTpx2 is not required for hKif15 processivity.
source: So far our experiments show that hTpx2 is not required for hKif15 to bind microtubules or for the motors processivity and ability to crosslink microtubules (as a tetramer).
evidence: Based on experiments showing hKif15 processivity in the absence of hTpx2.

claim: hTpx2 is not required for hKif15 ability to crosslink microtubules.
source: So far our experiments show that hTpx2 is not required for hKif15 to bind microtubules or for the motors processivity and ability to crosslink microtubules (as a tetramer).
evidence: Based on experiments showing hKif15 can crosslink microtubules in the absence of hTpx2.

claim: hTpx2 is essential for hKif15 to be recruited to the mitotic spindle.
source: However, cell-biological experiments showed that hTpx2 is essential for hKif15 to be recruited to the mitotic spindle (Tanenbaum et al., 2009; Vanneste et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to published cell biological studies.

claim: At nanomolar concentrations, hKif15 and hTpx2 do not form a complex in solution over a range of different salt conditions.
source: With nanomolar concentrations of each protein, we could not observe any complex formation over a range of different salt conditions (50 mM HEPES pH7.5, 0/150/300/450 mM NaCl [data not shown] and 35 mM sodium phosphate buffer [Figure 5A]).
evidence: Demonstrated by glycerol gradient ultracentrifugation shown in Figure 5A.

claim: A 30-fold excess of hTpx2 dimers allows the formation of a hKif15-hTpx2 complex of approximately 14.0S.
source: However, a 30-fold excess of hTpx2 dimers (2.5 µM hTpx2 [dimer] + 80 nM hKif15 [tetramer]) allowed the formation of a hKif15-hTpx2 complex of ∼14.0S, which included approximately one third of the provided hKif15 (Figure 5A, lower gels).
evidence: Demonstrated by glycerol gradient ultracentrifugation shown in Figure 5A, lower gels.

claim: The dissociation constant of the hKif15–hTpx2 complex is likely to be in the µM range.
source: The dissociation constant of the hKif15–hTpx2 complex is likely to be in the µM range arguing that its formation in vivo is less likely.
evidence: Inferred from the requirement of high µM concentrations of hTpx2 to form complex in solution.

claim: Formation of hKif15-hTpx2 complex in vivo is less likely based on the µM dissociation constant.
source: The dissociation constant of the hKif15–hTpx2 complex is likely to be in the µM range arguing that its formation in vivo is less likely.
evidence: Inferred from the high dissociation constant.

claim: At low nM concentrations, hTpx2 (30 nM, dimer) enhances the affinity of hKif15 (15 nM, tetramer) binding to GMP-CPP stabilised microtubules in the presence of AMP-PNP.
source: In contrast, using a microtubule sedimentation assay, we observed that at low nM concentrations, hTpx2 (30 nM, dimer) does enhance the affinity of hKif15 (15 nM, tetramer) binding to GMP-CPP stabilised microtubules when in the presence of the non-hydrolysable ATP analogue AMP-PNP (the fitted Kd increasing ∼twofold from 993 nM to 490 nM; Figure 5B).
evidence: Demonstrated by microtubule sedimentation assay shown in Figure 5B.

claim: hTpx2 increases the Kd of hKif15 for microtubules approximately twofold from 993 nM to 490 nM.
source: In contrast, using a microtubule sedimentation assay, we observed that at low nM concentrations, hTpx2 (30 nM, dimer) does enhance the affinity of hKif15 (15 nM, tetramer) binding to GMP-CPP stabilised microtubules when in the presence of the non-hydrolysable ATP analogue AMP-PNP (the fitted Kd increasing ∼twofold from 993 nM to 490 nM; Figure 5B).
evidence: Measured by microtubule sedimentation assay with fitted Kd values shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The observation that hTpx2 enhances hKif15 microtubule binding affinity could explain why cell-biological experiments show that association of hKif15 with the mitotic spindle depends on hTpx2.
source: This observation could explain why cell-biological experiments show that association of hKif15 with the mitotic spindle depends on hTpx2 (Tanenbaum et al., 2009; Vanneste et al., 2009).
evidence: Inferred from the microtubule binding affinity data and cited cell biological observations.

claim: Addition of hTpx2 decreased the proportion of motile hKif15 motors on microtubules by 70%.
source: Addition of hTpx2 decreased the proportion of motile motors on microtubules by 70%.
evidence: Quantified by TIRF microscopy shown in Figure 5C.

claim: hTpx2 inhibition of hKif15 is not selective for either directional or diffusive movement.
source: The remaining motors still showed both directional and diffusive movement, indicating that inhibition by hTpx2 is not selective for either type of movement (Figure 5C, kymographs and left graph below).
evidence: Observed by TIRF microscopy shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The velocity distribution of hKif15 motors in the presence of hTpx2 shows a bimodal distribution.
source: Further, the velocity distribution of remaining processive motors (compared to Figure 2A) now shows a bimodal distribution with a high proportion of slow motors (42.1 ± 1.7 nm•s−1 median ± SEM) and fewer motors at the median speed of hKif15 motors in the absence of hTpx2 (114.9 ± 3.2 nm•s−1 median ± SEM) (Figure 5C, right graph below).
evidence: Measured by TIRF microscopy with velocity distribution shown in Figure 5C, right graph.

claim: In the presence of hTpx2, a high proportion of hKif15 motors move slowly at 42.1 ± 1.7 nm•s−1 (median ± SEM).
source: Further, the velocity distribution of remaining processive motors (compared to Figure 2A) now shows a bimodal distribution with a high proportion of slow motors (42.1 ± 1.7 nm•s−1 median ± SEM) and fewer motors at the median speed of hKif15 motors in the absence of hTpx2 (114.9 ± 3.2 nm•s−1 median ± SEM) (Figure 5C, right graph below).
evidence: Measured by TIRF microscopy with velocity distribution shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The bimodal velocity distribution in the presence of hTpx2 may reflect the higher probability of a fast moving motor engaging hTpx2 molecules bound on the microtubule lattice.
source: This may reflect the higher probability of a fast moving motor from engaging hTpx2 molecules that are bound on the microtubule lattice.
evidence: Inferred from the velocity distribution data in the presence of hTpx2.

claim: In the presence of hTpx2, hKif15 motors can no longer step processively but remain bound to the microtubule lattice.
source: The hKif15 motor could no-longer step processively, although it remained bound to the microtubule lattice (4/5 cases; Figures 5D, 2. blue trace).
evidence: Demonstrated by optical trap experiments shown in Figure 5D.

claim: In the presence of hTpx2, hKif15 can maintain microtubule attachment at forces that would have forced dissociation in the absence of hTpx2.
source: During this period, the bead can maintain microtubule attachment at forces that—in the absence of hTpx2—would have forced dissociation of the motor (compare also with Figure 2E).
evidence: Demonstrated by optical trap experiments comparing force tolerance with and without hTpx2 shown in Figure 5D and Figure 2E.

claim: hTpx2 increases the force-holding capability of microtubule-bound hKif15.
source: Thus, hTpx2 increases the force-holding capability of microtubule-bound hKif15.
evidence: Concluded from optical trap experiments showing maintained attachment at higher forces in presence of hTpx2.

claim: Kinesin-1 motility is unaffected by the presence of hTpx2.
source: We can rule out a generic 'roadblock' inhibition-mechanism: Firstly, kinesin-1 motility is unaffected by the presence of hTpx2 (n = 5; Figure 5D, green traces).
evidence: Demonstrated by optical trap experiments with kinesin-1 in presence of hTpx2 shown in Figure 5D.

claim: hTpx2 inhibits hKif15 motility at low nanomolar concentrations when only single molecules are present on the lattice.
source: Secondly, hTpx2 already inhibits hKif15 motility at low nanomolar concentrations when only single molecules are present on the lattice.
evidence: Observed in TIRF experiments at low motor concentrations.

claim: Inhibition of bead motility by hTpx2 is not simply mediated by hTpx2-bead-microtubule interactions.
source: Kinesin-1 motility in the presence of hTpx2 also shows that inhibition of bead motility in case of hKif15 is not simply mediated by hTpx2-bead-microtubule interactions.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that kinesin-1 is unaffected by hTpx2.

claim: hTpx2 is a selective inhibitor of hKif15 motor stepping presumably by forming stable trimeric hKif15-hTpx2-microtubule complexes.
source: Thus, hTpx2 is a selective inhibitor of hKif15 motor stepping presumably by forming stable trimeric hKif15-hTpx2-microtubule complexes.
evidence: Concluded from optical trap and TIRF data showing selective inhibition of hKif15 but not kinesin-1, and increased force-holding capability.

claim: hKif15 and Kif11 are only able to step under low loads in the 1–3 pN range.
source: Indeed, hKif15, like Kif11, is only able to step under low loads in the 1–3 pN range (Korneev et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by data for hKif15 and citation for Kif11.

claim: Both hKif15 and Kif11 motors are able to undergo plus-end-directed movement or 1-D diffusion.
source: However, our data show that Kif15 motors have a number of biophysical properties that distinguish it from Kif11: while both motors are able to undergo plus-end-directed movement or 1-D diffusion (Kwok et al., 2006; Kapitein et al., 2008; Figure 6, 'A'), the median velocity of hKif15 is 10-fold higher than that of Kif11 and processive runs have a fourfold longer duration (Korneev et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by data for hKif15 and citations for Kif11.

claim: The median velocity of hKif15 is 10-fold higher than that of Kif11.
source: However, our data show that Kif15 motors have a number of biophysical properties that distinguish it from Kif11: while both motors are able to undergo plus-end-directed movement or 1-D diffusion (Kwok et al., 2006; Kapitein et al., 2008; Figure 6, 'A'), the median velocity of hKif15 is 10-fold higher than that of Kif11 and processive runs have a fourfold longer duration (Korneev et al., 2007).
evidence: Based on comparison of measured hKif15 velocity with cited Kif11 velocity.

claim: hKif15 processive runs have a fourfold longer duration than Kif11.
source: However, our data show that Kif15 motors have a number of biophysical properties that distinguish it from Kif11: while both motors are able to undergo plus-end-directed movement or 1-D diffusion (Kwok et al., 2006; Kapitein et al., 2008; Figure 6, 'A'), the median velocity of hKif15 is 10-fold higher than that of Kif11 and processive runs have a fourfold longer duration (Korneev et al., 2007).
evidence: Based on comparison of measured hKif15 duration with cited Kif11 duration.

claim: For hKif15, both processive and diffusive movement types occur at the same ionic strength.
source: In the case of hKif15, both these movement types occur at the same ionic strength.
evidence: Demonstrated by TIRF microscopy at different salt concentrations.

claim: For Kif11, processive and diffusive movement is exclusive and depends on the ionic strength.
source: In contrast, processive and diffusive movement by Kif11 is exclusive and depends on the ionic strength (Kapitein et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to published study.

claim: Pauses during processive runs have not been reported for Kif11.
source: Additionally, to our knowledge, pauses during processive runs have not been reported for Kif11.
evidence: Based on review of published literature on Kif11.

claim: A switch by hKif15 starts with attachment of the second, free head-pair to the lattice of the intersecting microtubule, while the first, engaged head-pair stays attached to the old track.
source: As hKif15 is a motile tetramer, we propose that a switch starts with attachment of the second, free head-pair to the lattice of the intersecting microtubule, while the first, engaged head-pair of the same molecule stays attached to the old track.
evidence: Proposed mechanism based on tetrameric structure and switching observations.

claim: The hKif15 bridge at intersections can pause or resolve by detachment of the second domain-pair into a pass or by detachment of the first domain-pair into a switch event.
source: This hKif15 bridge can now pause at the intersection or resolve by detachment of the second domain-pair into a pass or by detachment of the firstdomain-pair into a switch event (Figure 6, 'B'+box).
evidence: Proposed mechanism based on switching observations and tetrameric structure.

claim: Microtubule switching is a feature that is very helpful to navigate through the complex microtubule arrangement within the k-fibre.
source: Microtubule switching is a feature that is very helpful to navigate through the complex microtubule arrangement within the k-fibre.
evidence: Inferred from switching capability and k-fibre structure.

claim: Each switch event is equivalent to a new independent run on a new microtubule.
source: Thereby each switch event is equivalent to a new independent run on a new microtubule, so that a single molecule can travel a distance of 'median run-length × (nswitches+1)' as we have shown in Figure 3C: traces C-E sum up to 7.4 µm run length in total, with single traces at 1.6, 3.7 and 2.1 µm.
evidence: Demonstrated by tracking single motor across multiple microtubules shown in Figure 3C.

claim: A single hKif15 molecule can travel a distance of 'median run-length × (nswitches+1)' through switching.
source: Thereby each switch event is equivalent to a new independent run on a new microtubule, so that a single molecule can travel a distance of 'median run-length × (nswitches+1)' as we have shown in Figure 3C: traces C-E sum up to 7.4 µm run length in total, with single traces at 1.6, 3.7 and 2.1 µm.
evidence: Calculated from observed switching behavior and run lengths shown in Figure 3C.

claim: A single hKif15 molecule would have a high probability of reaching the plus-end (kinetochores) of the k-fibre through switching.
source: Thus, even with a moderate median run length of 2 microns, a single molecule would have a high probability of reaching the plus-end (kinetochores) of the k-fibre, regardless of any discontinuity within the fibre or roadblocks owing to structural microtubule-associated elements (Figure 6, 'B'+box).
evidence: Inferred from switching capability and cumulative run length calculations.

claim: Short running, non-switching hKif11 cannot travel far enough into the k-fibre network to reach the kinetochore/plus-end.
source: In contrast, short running, non-switching hKif11, that additionally is constantly gathered at the spindle poles by a dynein-dependent minus-end-directed flux (Ma et al., 2010), cannot travel far enough into the k-fibre network to reach the kinetochore/plus-end.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of hKif11 properties with hKif15 and cited flux data.

claim: hKif11 is constantly gathered at the spindle poles by a dynein-dependent minus-end-directed flux.
source: In contrast, short running, non-switching hKif11, that additionally is constantly gathered at the spindle poles by a dynein-dependent minus-end-directed flux (Ma et al., 2010), cannot travel far enough into the k-fibre network to reach the kinetochore/plus-end.
evidence: Supported by citation to published study.

claim: hKif11 localises mainly to the spindle pole and fades towards the spindle midzone.
source: In vivo data backs up this hypothesis, as hKif11 localises mainly to the spindle pole and fades towards the spindle midzone, while hKif15 is localised uniformly along the k-fibres (Vanneste et al., 2009; Sturgill and Ohi, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to published localization studies.

claim: hKif15 is localised uniformly along the k-fibres.
source: In vivo data backs up this hypothesis, as hKif11 localises mainly to the spindle pole and fades towards the spindle midzone, while hKif15 is localised uniformly along the k-fibres (Vanneste et al., 2009; Sturgill and Ohi, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to published localization studies.

claim: Kif15 motors modulate the capacity of k-fibre microtubule bundles to generate an inward-directed force within the spindle in opposition to hKif11.
source: Moreover, Kif15 motors also modulate the capacity of k-fibre microtubule bundles to generate an inward-directed force within the spindle (in opposition to hKif11) (Sturgill and Ohi, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to published study.

claim: Due to their prolonged end dwell time, hKif15 motors may influence plus-end dynamics at kinetochores.
source: One possibility is that, due to their prolonged end dwell time, hKif15 motors may influence plus-end dynamics at kinetochores (Figure 6, 'C').
evidence: Speculated based on observed end dwell time and comparison with other motors.

claim: Kinesin-8 Kif18a dampens microtubule dynamics in vitro.
source: Such is the proposed role of the Kinesin-8 Kif18a, which is reported to dampen microtubule dynamics in vitro (Du et al., 2010; Stumpff et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies.

claim: hKif15 crosslinks may be reinforced by inhibitory hTpx2 turning dynamic hKif15 crosslinks into static structural hKif15/hTpx2 crosslinks.
source: Such cross-links may be reinforced by inhibitory hTpx2 (see below) turning dynamic hKif15 crosslinks into static structural hKif15/hTpx2 crosslinks that can resist higher forces than hKif15 only crosslinks (Figure 6, 'D'+box).
evidence: Inferred from hTpx2 inhibition data and increased force-holding capability.

claim: Static hKif15/hTpx2 crosslinks can resist higher forces than hKif15 only crosslinks.
source: Such cross-links may be reinforced by inhibitory hTpx2 (see below) turning dynamic hKif15 crosslinks into static structural hKif15/hTpx2 crosslinks that can resist higher forces than hKif15 only crosslinks (Figure 6, 'D'+box).
evidence: Inferred from optical trap data showing increased force tolerance with hTpx2.

claim: In vivo, other additional factors may be involved in hKif15-mediated extensile sliding of anti-parallel microtubules.
source: Our data does not, however, provide any evidence that hKif15 drives a Kif11-like continuous extensile sliding of anti-parallel microtubules in vitro, though we cannot rule out that in vivo other additional factors are involved in such an activity.
evidence: Speculated based on lack of in vitro evidence but known in vivo functions.

claim: The factor involved in hKif15-mediated sliding is unlikely to be hTpx2 since hTpx2 inhibits hKif15 stepping.
source: This factor is unlikely to be hTpx2 since our data shows this protein to inhibit the stepping of hKif15.
evidence: Inferred from data showing hTpx2 inhibits stepping.

claim: hTpx2 and hKif11 are constantly transported to the spindle pole.
source: How this mechanism is regulated within the spindle will be an important future work, but the fact that hTpx2 and hKif11 are constantly transported to the spindle pole (Ma et al., 2010) might hint to a partition of the spindle into a hKif11 active zone around the poles and a hKif15 active zone towards the spindle equator.
evidence: Supported by citation to published study.

claim: The spindle may be partitioned into a hKif11 active zone around the poles and a hKif15 active zone towards the spindle equator.
source: How this mechanism is regulated within the spindle will be an important future work, but the fact that hTpx2 and hKif11 are constantly transported to the spindle pole (Ma et al., 2010) might hint to a partition of the spindle into a hKif11 active zone around the poles and a hKif15 active zone towards the spindle equator.
evidence: Speculated based on differential localization and transport of hKif11/hTpx2 vs hKif15.

claim: hKif15 is a distinct class of kinesin that assembles into stable tetramers.
source: Overall, our data provide the first insight into the biochemical and biophysical properties of the full-length human Kinesin-12 hKif15. We reveal that hKif15 is a distinct class of kinesin that assembles into stable tetramers, which are highly processive, can navigate microtubule networks by switching track and form high load-bearing microtubule–microtubule crosslinks when bound to the regulatory factor hTpx2.
evidence: Supported by biochemical and biophysical characterization throughout the study.

claim: hKif15 tetramers are highly processive.
source: Overall, our data provide the first insight into the biochemical and biophysical properties of the full-length human Kinesin-12 hKif15. We reveal that hKif15 is a distinct class of kinesin that assembles into stable tetramers, which are highly processive, can navigate microtubule networks by switching track and form high load-bearing microtubule–microtubule crosslinks when bound to the regulatory factor hTpx2.
evidence: Demonstrated by TIRF microscopy showing long run lengths and residency times.

claim: hKif15 can navigate microtubule networks by switching track.
source: Overall, our data provide the first insight into the biochemical and biophysical properties of the full-length human Kinesin-12 hKif15. We reveal that hKif15 is a distinct class of kinesin that assembles into stable tetramers, which are highly processive, can navigate microtubule networks by switching track and form high load-bearing microtubule–microtubule crosslinks when bound to the regulatory factor hTpx2.
evidence: Demonstrated by TIRF microscopy showing track switching at intersections.

claim: hKif15 forms high load-bearing microtubule-microtubule crosslinks when bound to the regulatory factor hTpx2.
source: Overall, our data provide the first insight into the biochemical and biophysical properties of the full-length human Kinesin-12 hKif15. We reveal that hKif15 is a distinct class of kinesin that assembles into stable tetramers, which are highly processive, can navigate microtubule networks by switching track and form high load-bearing microtubule–microtubule crosslinks when bound to the regulatory factor hTpx2.
evidence: Demonstrated by optical trap experiments showing increased force tolerance with hTpx2.

claim: The hKIF15 ORF is toxic to E. coli cells when antibiotics other than ampicillin are used.
source: We observed that the hKIF15 ORF is toxic to Escherichia coli cells when antibiotics other than ampicillin (e.g., kanamycin, gentamycin) are used, so viral genome generation by the Invitrogen Bac-to-Bac system (Life Technologies, Paisley, UK) using DH10BAC cells is not possible.
evidence: Observed during cloning and expression plasmid construction.

claim: Viral genome generation of hKIF15 by the Invitrogen Bac-to-Bac system using DH10BAC cells is not possible.
source: We observed that the hKIF15 ORF is toxic to Escherichia coli cells when antibiotics other than ampicillin (e.g., kanamycin, gentamycin) are used, so viral genome generation by the Invitrogen Bac-to-Bac system (Life Technologies, Paisley, UK) using DH10BAC cells is not possible.
evidence: Concluded from toxicity observations during cloning.
